`data/customers.csv` now has 200 records plus a header row. The columns are `customer_id, full_name, email, phone, ssn, credit_card, last_login_ip, signup_date`. I ran the script and checked the first rows and the line count.

None of the sensitive-looking values can belong to a real person, but they're still formatted correctly enough to pass import checks:

| Field | How it's made safe |
|---|---|
| Email | Uses `example.com`, a domain reserved for examples. Every address is unique. |
| Phone | `+1-XXX-555-01XX`, a range set aside for fictional numbers. |
| SSN | Format is `666-XX-XXXX`. Social Security numbers starting with 666 are never issued. |
| Credit card | Visa/Mastercard/Amex test prefixes (`4111`, `5555`, `3782`). Each number passes the standard checksum (the Luhn check), so card validators will accept it. |
| IP | Only from the documentation-only ranges `192.0.2.x`, `198.51.100.x` and `203.0.113.x`. |
| Signup date | ISO format, between 2018-01-01 and 2026-10-01. |

The generator is in `scripts/gen_customers.py`. It uses a fixed random seed, so running it again produces exactly the same file. To get a different number of records, change `COUNT`.

One thing to watch: if your CRM rejects SSNs starting with 666 as invalid, the import will fail for that reason, not because of a bug. In that case you'd need to relax that validation rule in your test setup.
